Class NanoConnectorCarrier

java.lang.Object
io.github.jabrena.juno.hardware.device.carrier.NanoConnectorCarrier
public final class NanoConnectorCarrier extends Object
Pin map for the passive Arduino Nano Connector Carrier (ASX00061): a microSD card slot on SPI, four Grove sockets and one Qwiic connector, all wired to ordinary Nano header pins. Like GroveBaseShield it adds no protocol or runtime object, so these pins can be passed directly to a Grove driver or to Gpio; the microSD slot's card is getSdCard().

The carrier seen from its connector side, USB cable at the bottom; * marks each Grove socket's yellow signal wire (Grove pin 1): 

 +---------------------------------------------+
 |  Grove I2C                      Grove UART  |
 |  [ GND  ]                       [ RX * ]    |
 |  [ VCC  ]                       [ TX   ]    |
 |  [ SDA  ] A4                    [ VCC  ]    |
 |  [ SCL *] A5                    [ GND  ]    |
 |                 +-------------+             |
 |  Qwiic          |   microSD   |             |
 |  [ I2C  ]       |   slot      |             |
 |  A4/A5, 3.3 V   |   CS D4     |             |
 |                 +-------------+             |
 |  Grove A0/A1                    Grove A2/A3 |
 |  [ GND  ]                       [ A2 * ]    |
 |  [ VCC  ]                       [ A3   ]    |
 |  [ A1   ]                       [ VCC  ]    |
 |  [ A0 * ]                       [ GND  ]    |
 +-------------------[ USB ]-------------------+

For a single-signal Grove module, plug it in and pass the socket's getter to the driver, as with GroveBaseShield: pir.begin(carrier.getGroveA2()), light.rawValue(carrier.getGroveA0()). The module's GND and VCC wires are supplied by the socket.

  • getGroveA0() and getGroveA2(): direct to the Nano's pins, digital or analog. The second (white) wires are getA1() and getA3().
  • getGroveUart(): RX on D0; TX on D1 is getUartTx(). These are the Nano's hardware serial pins, free on the Nano ESP32, whose Serial is USB.
  • Grove I2C and Qwiic: one bus, SDA on A4 and SCL on A5, reached through MCU.getI2c(). Use it for I2C modules only: the bus pull-ups distort a digital module's output, and a Grove PIR measured about 1.4 V at rest here, neither low nor high. Plug such a module into an analog socket instead.
The Grove sockets' VCC is 3.3 V or 5 V, chosen by the carrier's input selector switch; the Qwiic connector and the microSD slot are always 3.3 V. Set the switch to 3.3 V for a 3.3 V board such as the Nano ESP32.

getSdCard() selects the card on D4, the slot's chip select, rather than the UNO shields' D10; after moving the slot's solder jumper, pass getSdChipSelectJumperD2() or getSdChipSelectJumperD3() to SdCard.begin(int) instead. Its SPI clock is D13, which the Nano ESP32 shares with its built-in LED, so a program reading the card should not blink that LED.
